newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong stocks return to lag Asia markets-Goldman.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong stocks return to lag Asia markets-Goldman.

text.p: Hong Kong share prices have climbed over 20 percent this year and investors may now turn to other regional markets for higher yields going forward, Goldman Sachs executive director Janice Wallace said on Friday.

"We have been overweight Hong Kong. The question now is not do you stay overweight but do you continue to put more money into Hong Kong at this level or do you look for other opportunities," Wallace told Reuters.
"From this level I would say Hong Kong certainly has less upside now given how much it has moved," said Wallace, who also shares the job as head of research.
Goldman's 12-month target for the Hong Kong's Hang Seng index is 13,000 points, about four percent higher than current levels, while returns in Asia could average 15 percent next year, Wallace said.
Goldman is currently overweight in Hong Kong, where share prices have surged to record levels following a switching out of other regional markets into Hong Kong.
"I think there will come a day when they (investors) want to be back in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia and other markets," Wallace said.
"The toughest call is whether we get more inflow overall...," she added.
Singapore could see the loftiest yields next year at around 20 percent, while Indonesia could also look attractive with returns close to 20 percent, Wallace said.
While South Korea could also show "terrific upside", gains may not materialise in the near term, and Thailand could see a recovery in the longer term after a number of false starts.
Improvements in the Chinese economy and a benign interest rate outlook in the United States have propelled the Hang Seng's recent rise, Wallace said.

While Goldman's 13,000 point target could be seen as conservative, she cautioned that it may take time for China to have an impact on Hong Kong's economy and U.S. interest rates are expected to pick up next year.
"That will also put a bit of a cap on Hong Kong as well."
Recovery in Hong Kong's residential property sector has given property development stocks a leading position in Hong Kong's rally, but Wallace said they may not hold that lead.

"We would say the residential developers are looking fairly fully priced. They have definitely been the best peformers and they are now trading all pretty close to net asset value or slightly above," she said.

"It is harder to see those stocks continuing to lead unless we get big liquidity from China buying residential (property) and quite honestly I think it is more likely that that will go into the commercial property sector," Wallace said.
She said Goldman liked Hong Kong conglomerates, which had broad-based exposure to the economic upturn, hotels and banks.
"There is still good growth in the banks and the reduction in mortgage pricing has stimulated the market," she said.
Wallace said Hong Kong's retail stocks still failed to excite. "We think we are sort of trundling along the bottom," she said of retail sales in the territory.

In the near term, Wallace said Hong Kong shares were likely to consolidate. "Short term it is hard to see Hong Kong getting another big move up from here unless we see a lot more money into the region," she said.
